title: Data Protection for Workflows — Module Quiz

items.q: Why draw the path personal data takes before reading any law?
options: Laws are easier to understand with diagrams
Obligations attach to data you hold or send, so you cannot say which duties apply without knowing where it goes
Regulators require a diagram before an investigation
items.explain: Every duty attaches to something you hold or send. The path shows which duties apply and where you cannot currently check you are meeting them.

items.q: Why can the text of a question put to an assistant be personal data?
options: Assistants are required to log every question
People volunteer details in free-text boxes, such as an age and a symptom, that you never asked for
Questions are always linked to a user account
items.explain: What people volunteer is rarely what you planned for. The question can contain health information, a name or an age.

items.q: Under the DPDP Act, does engaging a processor to handle data move responsibility to the processor?
options: Yes, once a valid contract is signed
No, the Data Fiduciary stays responsible, irrespective of any agreement to the contrary
Only for processing done outside India
items.explain: Section 8(1) keeps the fiduciary answerable for processing done on its behalf by a processor. Hiring someone does not hand over the responsibility.

items.q: Which of these is a place people commonly forget when mapping where personal data rests?
options: The main production database
Logs, backups, exports and the model provider
The login page
items.explain: Logs, backups, error reports, analytics, exports saved to a laptop, and the provider are second copies that nobody decided to create.

items.q: A workflow relies on 'legitimate interests' as its reason for using data. Which statement is accurate?
options: The DPDP Act has the same broad legitimate-interests basis as the GDPR
The DPDP Act works through consent or a short list of listed legitimate uses, with no direct equivalent
Neither law permits any reason other than consent
items.explain: The GDPR names six lawful bases, including legitimate interests. The DPDP Act's two routes are consent and listed legitimate uses.

items.q: Roughly when do the DPDP Act's main duties on data fiduciaries start, according to the summaries read?
options: They have applied since 2023
Staged, with the main duties around eighteen months after the Rules were notified in November 2025
They only apply to organisations based in India
items.explain: The summaries disagree by a day on dates and on section lists, so the Gazette notification is what to read. Not yet in force is no reason to wait to build well.

items.q: What does a penalty figure such as 'up to 250 crore rupees' tell you?
options: The usual penalty for any breach of the Act
A ceiling that shows how seriously the lawmakers regard the duty, not a prediction
A fixed fine that applies automatically
items.explain: Every figure reads 'may extend to'. Actual penalties depend on the facts and on how the regulator weighs them.

items.q: Who does each law's own territory limit?
options: Only organisations physically located there
Neither stops at a border; both can reach organisations offering services to people in their territory
Only organisations above a size threshold
items.explain: A site anyone in the world can open should assume more than one regime can be relevant, and which law actually applies is a question for advice.

items.q: Why is minimisation the cheapest protection available?
options: Regulators exempt organisations that hold little data
Data you never collected cannot be breached, needs no erasure on request, and needs no contract with a recipient
Smaller datasets are always more accurate
items.explain: Every duty is easier to meet if you hold less. It is also good engineering and not only a legal duty.

items.q: A redactor catches email-shaped and phone-shaped text. What does it miss?
options: Nothing that matters
Names, addresses written in prose, and details described in words
Anything longer than one sentence
items.explain: A pattern is a net and not a wall. It reduces the obvious cases and leaves the rest, so describe it as no more than that.

items.q: A step summarises complaints. What is the best way to keep customer names away from the model?
options: Ask the model not to repeat names
Give each record an opaque reference and let your code join the reply back to the customer
Let the model see names but delete its logs
items.explain: The model supplies content and your code supplies the target. The identifying detail stays on the side of the boundary you control.

items.q: Why does storing the shape of a call and not the question make repurposing impossible?
options: Shapes are encrypted by default
The content that could be mined was never recorded, which is stronger than a policy against mining it
Regulators forbid analysis of call shapes
items.explain: Not storing the content removes the retention period, the deletion path, the access controls and the temptation.

items.q: Why might the same API call be under different privacy terms from one plan to another?
options: Providers change the model weights for paid users
Terms can differ by plan, so switching billing on or off can change what happens to submitted content
Terms apply only to the first call in a session
items.explain: The same code can sit under quite different data terms depending on the plan. Read the terms for the plan you are actually on.

items.q: What must an assurance given to users satisfy?
options: It must be reassuring and short
It must be true on the plan actually in use, today
It must match what competitors say
items.explain: An assurance that is true only on a plan you have not bought is a false statement, and a promise about children's questions that might be false is worse than none.

items.q: What did the footer on Lrnon's assistant promise that could not be verified?
options: That answers were always correct
That nothing a learner typed was used to train anything, when the provider's terms for the plan in use were unchecked
That questions were deleted after one hour
items.explain: The footer now states only what holds on any plan: that the question is sent to an outside AI service and that people should not type personal details.

items.q: If the data involves other people's personal details, which provider plan is the wrong choice?
options: A paid plan whose terms say content is not used to improve products
A plan whose terms tell users not to submit personal information
Any plan with a usage limit
items.explain: Match the plan to the data, or change the data. Moving to a paid tier is often cheap against the risk.

items.q: Why does deleting a record from the main table not delete a person's data?
options: Main tables are read-only
Logs, backups, exports, caches, analytics and the processor all hold their own copies
Deletion only takes effect after thirty days
items.explain: Systems make copies without anyone deciding to, and each has its own life. A deletion has to reach all of them.

items.q: After restoring a backup, what must happen for earlier deletions to hold?
options: Nothing, because backups never contain deleted people
Deletions made since the snapshot are re-applied, so restored data does not bring deleted people back
The backup must be re-encrypted
items.explain: This step is the most often missing, and is the difference between a deletion that holds and one that quietly reverses.

items.q: Under DPDP section 8(7), when must personal data be erased?
options: Only when a court orders it
When consent is withdrawn or it is reasonable to assume the purpose is no longer served, unless a law requires retention
After exactly one year in all cases
items.explain: The fiduciary must also cause its processor to erase what it was given.

items.q: Who counts as a child under the DPDP Act?
options: Anyone under thirteen
Anyone under sixteen
Anyone under eighteen
items.explain: That is a higher line than many people assume and covers most teenagers using a service. Section 9 requires verifiable parental consent before processing a child's data.

items.q: A parent consents to a platform tracking their child's behaviour. What does section 9(3) say?
options: The consent makes the tracking lawful
The bar on tracking and behavioural monitoring applies to the processing itself, unless a specific exemption is prescribed
Tracking is allowed for children over sixteen
items.explain: Parental consent does not unlock tracking or behavioural monitoring. The exemptions are narrow and tied to particular purposes.

items.q: What is the GDPR's default age at which a child may consent themselves to an online service?
options: Thirteen everywhere
Sixteen, which Member States may lower to no less than thirteen
Eighteen
items.explain: So the age differs from one EU country to another, and a service operating across Europe has to know which applies.

items.q: What is the cheapest way to meet rules on children's data?
options: A clause in the terms saying the service is for adults
Designing so the restricted processing is not done at all
Asking users to confirm their age
items.explain: A service that needs no account, has no messaging or advertising and records no questions has little for the rules to bite on.

items.q: Why is a rights request itself a possible route to harm?
options: Requests always overload the support team
Someone may pose as another person to obtain their data or to have it deleted
Regulators publish the names of people who make requests
items.explain: Verify proportionately, and do not ask for more identifying detail than you need to confirm who is asking.

items.q: Why is answering a 'what do you hold about me' request from the main database alone risky?
options: Main databases are slow to search
It misses copies in logs, exports, backups and the processor, so the answer may be incomplete without saying so
Databases cannot export data
items.explain: Being incomplete is worse than saying what you could not search. A current data map is what makes a complete answer possible.

items.q: Is a promise to reply to feedback within two working days the same as a rights-request deadline?
options: Yes, it satisfies the legal period
No, a rights request has its own clock under the applicable law, separate from a service promise
Only for requests from outside the country
items.explain: A fast reply to a message is good practice. A rights request has its own deadline, record and consequences if missed.

items.q: What does GDPR Article 33 require after a personal data breach?
options: Notify every affected person within 24 hours
Notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours, unless it is unlikely to risk people's rights and freedoms
Notify the regulator only if more than a thousand people are affected
items.explain: A late notification must give reasons, a processor must tell the controller without undue delay, and every breach is to be documented, including ones not reported.

items.q: Why preserve evidence before cleaning up after a breach?
options: Regulators demand an unmodified server
A tidy-up that destroys the trail makes it impossible to assess what happened and who was affected
Evidence is needed to sell to insurers
items.explain: Contain first, then preserve, then assess. Assessment depends on the logs.
